content: Hypolipidemic agents, also known as antihyperlipidemic agents, are a diverse group of pharmaceutical drugs used to treat hyperlipidemias, which are conditions characterized by elevated levels of lipids in the blood. These medications are often referred to as lipid-lowering drugs (LLDs) or agents. Classes of Hypolipidemic Drugs There are several classes of hypolipidemic drugs, each with distinct effects on the cholesterol profile and potential adverse effects. Some drugs are more effective at lowering low-density lipoprotein (LDL), commonly referred to as bad cholesterol, while others may preferentially increase high-density lipoprotein (HDL), known as good cholesterol. The choice of a specific agent is determined by the patient’s cholesterol profile, cardiovascular risk, and liver and kidney function, with careful consideration of the risks and benefits of the medication. In the United States, this decision-making process is guided by evidence-based guidelines from the National Cholesterol Education Program (NCEP) Adult Treatment Panel III (ATP III). Statins Statins are particularly effective at lowering LDL cholesterol, which is strongly associated with cardiovascular diseases. Clinical studies have shown that standard doses of statins can reduce LDL cholesterol levels by 18% to 55%, depending on the specific statin used. However, statins carry a risk of severe muscle damage, including myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Fibrates Fibrates are primarily indicated for the treatment of hypertriglyceridemia. They typically reduce triglyceride levels by 20% to 50% and also increase HDL cholesterol levels. While fibrates may lower LDL cholesterol, their effect on LDL is generally less pronounced compared to statins. Similar to statins, fibrates carry a risk of severe muscle damage, including myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Niacin Niacin, like fibrates, is effective in lowering triglycerides by 20% to 50%. It can also reduce LDL cholesterol by 5% to 25% and increase HDL cholesterol by 15% to 35%. However, niacin may cause hyperglycemia and has the potential to induce liver damage. Bile Acid Sequestrants (Resins) Bile acid sequestrants are particularly effective at lowering LDL cholesterol by 15% to 30%. They achieve this by binding to cholesterol-containing bile acids in the gut, preventing their reabsorption. These agents also raise HDL cholesterol by 3% to 5%. However, they have minimal effect on triglycerides and may even cause a slight increase. Bile acid sequestrants can lead to gastrointestinal issues and may interfere with the absorption of other drugs and vitamins from the gut. Ezetimibe Ezetimibe (Zetia) is a selective inhibitor of dietary cholesterol absorption in the intestine. It is often used to lower LDL cholesterol levels. Phytosterols Phytosterols are naturally occurring compounds found in plants. Similar to ezetimibe, they reduce cholesterol absorption in the gut and are most effective when consumed with meals. However, the mechanism of action of phytosterols differs from that of ezetimibe. Investigational Classes of Hypolipidemic Agents CETP Inhibitors Cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitors are an investigational class of drugs still under development. These agents are expected to primarily increase HDL cholesterol while also lowering LDL cholesterol.
